item.title: The Daily Star – Why garment workers remain trapped in wage struggles
item.description:
Once again, ready-made garment (RMG) workers have taken to the streets to demand higher wages, as rising living costs have become a burden for them. Workers took to the streets in the same way in 2018 and 2023: this is a recurring pattern. It is unfortunate that the state has failed to take effective measures to ensure fair compensation and improve the well-being of workers in this sector. 

Since 1985, the minimum wage for the RMG sector has been revised a total of seven times: it was initially Tk 627, then Tk 930 in 1994, Tk 1,663 in 2006, Tk 3,000 in 2010, Tk 5,300 in 2013, Tk 8,000 in 2018 and Tk 12,500 in 2023. The 2023 increase drew mixed reactions from stakeholders. Labour unions argued that the rise was insufficient given inflation and the rising cost of living, while factory owners raised concerns about financial strain amid global economic challenges. 
Readymade garment workers block a road at Mirpur 10 roundabout in Dhaka on 31 October 2026, demanding a monthly minimum wage of Tk 30,000. Similar protests took place in 2018 and 2023, reflecting recurring disputes over wages. Photo: Mehedi Hasan

Discussions among the main stakeholders have centred on whether all factories have the capacity to implement the new wage and on the debate over a living wage. While minimum wage increases can lead to higher wages and greater bargaining power for workers, they may also have unintended consequences, such as reduced employment, more unpaid overtime and problems with compliance. Against this background, I led a research team to explore the impact of the minimum wage rise on workers, the challenges of implementing the new wage structure and stakeholders' perceptions of the current wage system. 

To understand wage governance, we need to analyse how the three main stakeholders (workers, factories and brands) perceived and experienced the 2023 minimum wage rise.

First, how did the 2023 wage rise affect workers? According to our research, funded by STITCH, workers' average income rose by 32.8% in 2024 compared with 2023. However, everyday expenses also rose over the same period: education by 32.64%, groceries by 28.86%, healthcare by 22.27% and rent by 9.96%. Comparing real wages between 2018 and 2023, the study found that despite substantial nominal increases, real wages in 2023 were about 12–15% lower than in 2018: workers' purchasing power had declined. This means that the higher income did not significantly improve workers' well-being because their expenses also increased amid the country's high inflation. In short, while nominal wages show dramatic increases, real wages have fallen once inflation is taken into account.

In the survey, workers were also asked whether their workload had changed after the new minimum wage was announced. Some 65.68% of workers reported a heavier workload in 2024 than in 2023. As one worker explained, "The pressure to produce more since they are paying more is there. As they are paying higher wages, they expect more work, so the workload has increased." Such dynamics place workers in a precarious position, as non-compliance often leads to reprimands or threats of job loss. 
Women operate sewing machines at a garment factory in Bangladesh. Although the minimum wage revision brought higher pay, 65.68% of surveyed workers reported heavier workloads, raising questions about whether wage increases have improved working conditions. Photo: Mehedi Hasan

One worker vented her frustration at length: " We wake up at 5, shower, get ready and go to work, all to put food on the table. Even after working hard and doing our jobs properly, if we do not receive our rightful wages, it is partly because we fail to demand them. We don't get what we deserve because we cannot stand up for our rights. It's like a mother who doesn't give her baby milk until the baby cries. So, if something isn't given to you, you have to demand it."

While the frustration and anger of the workers are evident, our study also shows that factories have struggled to adapt to the new minimum wage. Factories' wage costs rose by 31%, while 25% of factories reported receiving fewer orders from buyers than in 2023. As a result, factories' profit margins fell from 12.61% in 2022 to 7.34% in 2024, making it harder for them to adjust to the higher production costs brought about by the revised wage. The usual way to cover higher production costs is to raise the price of the product, which is very difficult in a buyer-driven sector. 

Our factory survey found very limited support from buyers: 67.11% of factories reported receiving no price increase from them. Factories often rely on buyers to adjust prices in response to wage increases, but buyers prioritise cost minimisation, which strains supplier-buyer relationships. Inconsistent price adjustments, buyers' leverage in negotiating lower costs and the absence of long-term collaboration leave suppliers financially unstable and hinder wage compliance. As one factory representative put it, "If the buyers just pay 5 cents more, it will have a big impact." Production costs in the RMG industry are rising as factories meet the social and environmental compliance standards of importing countries, yet the prices of Bangladeshi garments have been falling for more than a decade. Where is the shared responsibility?
Officials and representatives attend a Minimum Wage Board meeting on 4 November 2026. Despite formal representation, workers continue to have limited influence over wage-setting decisions, highlighting persistent imbalances in Bangladesh's wage governance system. Photo: Ministry of Labour and Employment

We also found that buyers wanted factories to tell them how much the wage revision would increase costs and how much of that increase would be reflected in product prices. According to the buyers, factories were uncomfortable with these discussions because they were unwilling to share their costs transparently. Buyers asked not only for the wages of graded workers but also for other operating costs, such as utilities and imported materials. Factories say that sharing all this information with buyers puts them in a weaker position when negotiating prices. According to one brand representative, " They (factories) just want a lump-sum increase of 5–10% in product prices. They say their operating costs have increased by Tk 30, 40 or 50 lakh. They do not want to disclose the exact costs; none of the factories agreed to share this information. Nevertheless, we have agreed to price increases of 2–3% and are implementing them." It seems to me that there is a lack of transparency and a systematic price adjustment mechanism, particularly when wages rise.

In my view, the government's role has received little attention in the experiences of workers, factories and brands during the minimum wage revision. The Wage Board is theoretically designed as a tripartite body with balanced representation from workers, employers and the government. However, significant power imbalances persist, leaving worker representatives with limited influence and further marginalising their role in policy discussions. Worker representation in wage-setting is an important but underdeveloped part of wage governance in Bangladesh. Despite the formal inclusion of worker representatives on the Wage Board, their selection process, political affiliations and lack of independence often undermine their ability to genuinely advocate for workers' interests. The exclusion of civil society organisations, trade unions and independent advocacy groups further weakens worker representation. 
For garment workers, the threat of unpaid wages, retaliatory dismissals and sudden factory closures remains a persistent source of insecurity, underscoring the need for stronger labour protections and effective wage governance. Photo: Anisur Rahman

Bangladesh has no national minimum wage or wage floor, which is where the problem begins. The minimum wage should have been set through open discussion. Even before Wage Board meetings, an open discussion could be organised involving civil society, brands, development agencies, the government, trade associations, unions, rights-based organisations, research institutions and owners of small, medium and large factories. As a labour institute argued, the model should allow all stakeholders, including the independent members of the Wage Board, to present data and enable the board to consider every aspect: technical, socioeconomic and business viability. The Purchasing Power Index should be taken into account when revising wages, and brands could adopt fair pricing mechanisms that reflect the actual cost of wage reforms. The most important factor missing from this process is the government's active involvement, as it tends to leave workers and factory owners to resolve disputes between themselves. This allows loopholes in wage governance to persist and this unruly pattern to continue, even though the government could play a stronger and more decisive role in the matter.

Shahidur Rahman is a professor at BRAC University and author of Broken Promises of Globalisation: The Case of the Bangladesh Garment Industry.

item.title: The Daily Star – Britain's love affair with curry and its colonial past
item.description:
In 2019, American academic Tim Nichols’ post on Twitter (now X), ‘Indian food is terrible and we pretend it isn’t’, sparked outrage across social media, raising concerns about racism, prejudice and the alienation of immigrants. Amidst a flurry of opinions both for and against, Britons emerged as some of the staunchest defenders of Indian cuisine. While Indian dishes are often a weekly staple in British households, with the much-loved pilau rice, madras, kormas, rogan joshes, jalfrezis, tikka masalas, samosas and bhajis sold as ready meals in supermarkets, the observance of ‘National Curry Week’ is an annual affair. The British nation’s fascination with Indian food had begun to take root during the eighteenth century as it emerged as a burgeoning imperial power; an appreciation of ‘curry’ thus often requires an appraisal of its more complex and, in many cases, unsavoury histories.

Beginnings of a culinary romance

Food is an inextricable part of colonial encounters and was central to experiencing foreign cultures. As Lizzie Collingham has shown, Edward Terry, chaplain at the embassy of Sir Thomas Roe to the Mughal court of Jahangir, was mesmerised by the sight of rice dishes served at banquets. While such high-end culinary adventures were awe-inspiring, ordinary everyday experiences were not short of wonder. James Forbes, who first arrived in 1765 at less than sixteen years of age to work as an East India Company writer, was fascinated by foodstuffs in western India. He documented natural life in his surroundings through text and images, and was particularly attentive to vegetables, grains and fruits. Adorning his thirteen-volume manuscripts and monumental four-volume Oriental Memoirs, pictures of local produce captured not only the diversity of India’s nature and culture but also how the coloniser wished to view them.
 
A portrait of James Forbes, published as the frontispiece to the first volume of his Oriental Memoirs in 1813. His writings and illustrations documented aspects of Indian society, culture and natural history.

A particular item that attracted Forbes’ attention was the mango, which he was strongly in favour of importing to England. He had struggled to explain the taste of mangoes in letters to his friends and family but depicted the fruit in a familiar still-life format so that it could immediately appeal to a European audience as an exotic delight. Forbes was also intrigued by Indian cooking techniques, especially how spices were prepared, combined and stirred into delicious, curried concoctions. If curries might have tantalised Forbes’ taste buds, the delectable sweetness of mangoes would have soothed his constitution, as he was keen on several recipes involving mangoes, from preserves to chutneys and everything in between.

A spicy dalliance deepens

While the British and other Europeans have understood curry as quintessentially South Asian, the concept of curry itself is rather unfamiliar to Indians in the subcontinent. Some writings have pointed to the Tamil word ‘kari’ or the Portuguese adaptation ‘caril’, but stews, relishes and gravies eaten all over South Asia are far too varied to be generalised as such. When I spotted curry powder on supermarket shelves for the first time in my life after arriving in continental Europe as a university student, I was a bit surprised – and disappointed when I checked the list of ingredients on the label. Finding good-quality garam masala was no easy feat either; but it was less of an issue, as every family has its own unique blend of spices that are sourced from specialist suppliers and then carefully threshed, roasted, powdered and stored in sealed containers.
 
James Forbes’ illustration of mangoes from Oriental Memoirs (1813), reflecting his interest in India’s natural history and the botanical observations recorded during his travels.

My own culinary curiosity, coupled with the need to introduce and discuss Indian food with European coursemates and colleagues, made me explore curry powder further and led me back again to the eighteenth century. Curry powder emerged in this era, as Indian food increasingly interested Britons. Linda Colley, in her book Captives: Britain, Empire, and the World, 1600–1850, mentions Sarah Shade, who, having confronted war and conflict in India, catered to the oriental tastes of British officials returning home by serving vegetable curries. The frontispiece of Hannah Glasse’s cookbook, featuring the recipe ‘To make a Currey the Indian Way’, shows a scullery maid in the background who is about to prepare poultry, perhaps to cook a chicken curry. Both meat and vegetarian options were already on the menu. In 1810, Sake Dean Mahomed went on to establish Britain’s first curry house in Portman Square, London.

A complicated relationship

Beneath the British obsession with curries, however, lie narratives that mostly escape our attention. While elaborate balls, feasts and parties were indispensable to the social lives of colonial officials, restrictions had come to be imposed on Indian royalty and nobility. For example, the Nawab of Murshidabad, Mubarak ud-Daulah, faced stark criticism from Governor-General Warren Hastings for his spending on local religious festivities; in fact, these acts of patronage had been integral to rulers’ obligations to their subjects for ages. 
 
Nawab Mubarak ud-Daulah receives the British Resident, Sir John Hadley D’Oyly, at his court in Murshidabad. The late eighteenth-century painting depicts a ruler whose spending on local religious festivities drew criticism from Governor-General Warren Hastings. Source: British Library/Wikimedia Commons

At the other end of the social scale, colonial extraction resulted in famines and outbreaks of diseases that destabilised Indian society and its economy. Farmers and cultivators were disparaged as either being too lazy, given the fertility of the soil, or their never-ending toil was highlighted as the plight of living under despotic governments. 

However, as almost 150 years of Indian economic scholarship has shown, it was the overweening tax burden of the Raj that reduced investment and productivity on the land. In such a scenario, it is hardly surprising that the introduction of new high-calorie crops such as potatoes was often championed as a boon of British governance. A later, exiled Nawab of Lucknow, Wajid Ali Shah, was reputed to have incorporated potatoes into his household’s biryani both as a response to fiscal pressure and as a culinary innovation. The variation remains a Bengali delicacy.

By the late 1780s, as the British had already begun to distance themselves from Indian life and culture, their attitude towards Indian cuisine also began to change. The diplomatic exchange of fruits, practised widely amongst Indian rulers, lost its sentimental value as the colonial state cultivated an image of being free from corruption. Food gifts also became a source of colonial anxiety, as Lord Valentia, during his travels across northern India, was baffled by the opulence of the delicacies presented to him by local dignitaries and often gave them away to his native servants. 
 
Sake Dean Mahomed (1759–1851), born in Patna, Bihar, was an Indian traveller, writer and entrepreneur who helped introduce Indian cuisine and culture to Britain.

The second half of the nineteenth century saw the British gradually shifting towards European menus at banquets in India, especially with French haute cuisine gaining pride of place. Not coincidentally, these social circles spent their summers in hill stations very close to tea plantations.

Curries, nevertheless, remained popular back in Britain. As Queen Victoria assumed the title of Empress of India in 1876, her interest in Indian life found expression in the magnificent Durbar Room at Osborne House. She was also fond of curry. Curries soon entered middle-class households and became part of the British imagination, so much so that, for instance, they were among Sherlock Holmes's favourite dishes. In The Adventure of Silver Blaze, the reference to curry helped the detective crack a mysterious case of intoxication. Holmes also feasted on a plate of curried fowl prepared by the housekeeper in the happy ending to The Adventure of the Naval Treaty. 
The first recipe for curry published in Britain appeared in Hannah Glasse’s The Art of Cookery Made Plain and Easy in 1747. Shown here are the book’s frontispiece and the original recipe. Source: Wikimedia Commons

Curry's widespread popularity, however, came at a cost. While the adaptation of individual recipes to local palates is inevitable, the twentieth-century practice of branding curries in eateries as mild, medium and hot has obscured much of their culinary diversity. Besides their socio-cultural complexities, Indian food takes a great deal of thought, labour and time to prepare. Reducing curries to 'sauces' and naming them after regions might seem efficient, but is ultimately a disservice to the ethos of South Asian communities that have treasured diverse culinary knowledge, methods and techniques across multiple lands and generations.

Healthy boundaries beyond curry

In line with developments in other disciplines, curry enthusiasts now talk about decolonising the cuisine. Amidst such deliberations, let's try to go beyond the 'curry' label and ask ourselves: are there any decent South Asian dishes other than curries? There are so many of them that one would never even need to fabricate something like Jamdani Haansh ('duck in sari'), favoured by Nessa in the British sitcom Gavin and Stacey! With the Indian food scene rapidly changing in the West, one might be pleasantly surprised by the diversity of dishes available beyond the familiar curry.
 
The cover of Linda Colley’s Captives: Britain, Empire and the World 1600–1850, published by Pimlico in 2003.

Transcending the limits of curry would also help us find inspiration in South Asian cultures' emphasis on cooking with diverse plant-based ingredients. This is important partly because the link between regular consumption of ultra-processed foods and the incidence of chronic diseases has now been well established. Gut health experts have come to suggest increasing the variety of plants we eat on a weekly basis, advocating the inclusion of herbs and spices in our regular diets. The adaptation of diverse diets thus requires us to acknowledge and engage more meaningfully with the cultural diversity around us.

Thinking about the history of 'curry' in this way must go beyond textual documentation stripped of its social and colonial contexts, or the mere recreation of past recipes. Instead, it would be essential to shed light on the cultural aesthetics of the various ingredients and their emotional and sensory dimensions. Learning about Indian cuisine on its own terms would be a productive way to enrich discussions on multiculturalism, food resilience, sustainability, nutrition and more inclusive futures.

Dr Apurba Chatterjee is a Visiting Research Fellow in the Department of History at the University of Reading, UK.

Holmes also feasted on a plate of curried fowl prepared by the housekeeper in the happy ending to The Adventure of the Naval Treaty.

Curry's widespread popularity, however, came at a cost. While the adaptation of individual recipes to local palates is inevitable, the twentieth-century practice of branding curries in eateries as mild, medium and hot has obscured much of their culinary diversity. Besides their socio-cultural complexities, Indian food takes a great deal of thought, labour and time to prepare. Reducing curries to 'sauces' and naming them after regions might seem efficient, but is ultimately a disservice to the ethos of South Asian communities that have treasured diverse culinary knowledge, methods and techniques across multiple lands and generations.

Healthy boundaries beyond curry

In line with developments in other disciplines, curry enthusiasts now talk about decolonising the cuisine. Amidst such deliberations, let's try to go beyond the 'curry' label and ask ourselves: are there any decent South Asian dishes other than curries? There are so many of them that one would never even need to fabricate something like Jamdani Haansh ('duck in sari'), favoured by Nessa in the British sitcom Gavin and Stacey! With the Indian food scene rapidly changing in the West, one might be pleasantly surprised by the diversity of dishes available beyond the familiar curry.

Transcending the limits of curry would also help us find inspiration in South Asian cultures' emphasis on cooking with diverse plant-based ingredients. This is important partly because the link between regular consumption of ultra-processed foods and the incidence of chronic diseases has now been well established. Gut health experts have come to suggest increasing the variety of plants we eat on a weekly basis, advocating the inclusion of herbs and spices in our regular diets. The adaptation of diverse diets thus requires us to acknowledge and engage more meaningfully with the cultural diversity around us.

Thinking about the history of 'curry' in this way must go beyond textual documentation stripped of its social and colonial contexts, or the mere recreation of past recipes. Instead, it would be essential to shed light on the cultural aesthetics of the various ingredients and their emotional and sensory dimensions. Learning about Indian cuisine on its own terms would be a productive way to enrich discussions on multiculturalism, food resilience, sustainability, nutrition and more inclusive futures.

The BoB connects South Asia and Southeast Asia, stretching from the Indian Ocean towards maritime pathways to the Pacific, and serves as a vital sea lane for shipping and energy transportation. Port development and naval security have assumed greater salience for many of these nations, including India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Myanmar. Arguably, the Bay has transitioned from a largely regional maritime space to a strategically contested space within the Indo-Pacific.

Given the political jostling in the Indo-Pacific, there has also been a distinct increase in interest among external powers in the BoB. This strategic transformation has occurred at the expense of internal cohesion, and it is often observed that the BoB nations are being drawn into the geopolitics of the Indo-Pacific.

The region has seen a plethora of initiatives, such as the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC, 1997) and the Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA, 1997), apart from several national initiatives, including India's MAHASAGAR initiative. Each of these subregional groupings and initiatives has focused on different stages of activities and interests, but given their nature, none of the subregional groupings or national projects can fully represent the larger Bay of Bengal identity and its common interests.

The historical significance of the Bay of Bengal: A forgotten maritime world

At the popular level, the history of the Bay of Bengal has largely remained confined to historical accounts and academic scholarship, attracting only intermittent interest from historians and occasional research initiatives. For centuries, the Bay of Bengal functioned as a maritime highway linking the Indian subcontinent with China and Southeast Asia. It subsequently became an arena of imperial competition, particularly with the expansion of European colonial powers. Shaped by the monsoon winds, maritime commerce and successive waves of human migration, the Bay facilitated the movement of people, ideas, religions and cultural practices across its shores. Yet, this emphasis on interconnectedness has often overshadowed the political rivalries, strategic contestations and competing interests that also shaped its maritime history and have typified contemporary international politics.

These movements across the Bay transformed patterns of trade and commerce, influenced social customs and created shared cultural understandings among communities separated by geography. Over time, however, many of these connections receded from collective memory, surviving largely through fragments of architectural heritage, food traditions, religious practices and local livelihood patterns. Traders and migrants from the Indian subcontinent left enduring imprints across the wider region, extending into present-day Southeast Asia. Port cities such as Singapore and Penang emerged as important centres of commercial activity and cultural diversity, reflecting the cosmopolitan character of the maritime world that developed around the Bay. Revisiting this history is therefore more than an exercise in historical recovery; it offers an important perspective for understanding contemporary regional connectivity projects and the possibilities of renewed cooperation, especially over some core interests.

In Crossing the Bay of Bengal, historian Sunil Amrith estimates that approximately 28 million people crossed the Bay in both directions between 1840 and 1940. Despite the magnitude of this movement, this remains one of the relatively underexplored chapters in the history of global migration. The nineteenth and early twentieth centuries witnessed an extraordinary movement of ordinary people, including indentured labourers, penal transportees and impoverished communities displaced by economic hardship and political circumstances. The subsequent collapse of the imperial order, the disruption of established trading networks and the redrawing of national boundaries fundamentally altered this maritime landscape. The political reorganisation of the twentieth century progressively dismantled many of the connections that had linked South and Southeast Asia for centuries. As Amrith observes, a region historically defined by mobility was increasingly fragmented by restrictions on trade, migration and cross-border movement. The Bay's earlier significance as an interconnected maritime space gradually diminished as the emerging nation-states prioritised territorial sovereignty and national boundaries over older networks of regional exchange.
Cover of Crossing the Bay of Bengal: The Furies of Nature and the Fortunes of Migrants published by Harvard University Press in 2013.

The twentieth century, therefore, marked a profound geopolitical transition in the history of the Bay of Bengal. Its significance did not disappear altogether, but its historical role as a corridor of human and commercial interaction became less visible in the emerging regional order. Amrith's larger historical argument is that the Bay of Bengal was part of a globalised world long before the Atlantic became the principal reference point in narratives of globalisation. Recovering this history is essential not only to understanding the region's past but also to reimagining its contemporary strategic, economic and commercial relevance.

Competition over common resources

The Bay of Bengal possesses considerable natural resources, particularly reserves of petroleum and natural gas. The shared exploitation of its marine resources has historically served as a source of interconnectedness among littoral states, but has also increasingly become a source of contestation. The Bay's waters support substantial fishing activity, with more than six million tonnes of seafood, including shrimp, crabs, prawns, tuna and small fish, reportedly harvested annually, accounting for approximately seven per cent of global fisheries production. However, growing demand, coupled with overexploitation and inadequate fisheries management, has placed considerable pressure on these resources. Declining fish catches, disruptions to marine ecosystems, biodiversity loss and increasing marine pollution have emerged as major environmental concerns, underscoring the need for coordinated regional action.

These competing demands on shared marine resources have also contributed to the growing fragmentation of what was historically an interconnected maritime region. Fishing disputes and disagreements over access to marine resources have long complicated bilateral relations, particularly between India and Sri Lanka, and India and Bangladesh. Although maritime boundary disputes between India and Myanmar and between India and Bangladesh have been settled, periodic incidents involving fishermen crossing into neighbouring waters continue to generate bilateral tensions, arrests and concerns over the treatment and human rights of detained fishermen. The problem is further compounded by weak fisheries governance and the absence of effective regional mechanisms to regulate fishing activity and protect vulnerable marine species. Despite receiving considerable international attention, these concerns remain largely unresolved, reflecting both the intensity of competing resource demands and the limited capacity of regional institutions to facilitate collective management.

Beyond fisheries, the Bay of Bengal has emerged as an increasingly important source of energy security. It is home to the world's largest deep-sea submarine fan, the Bengal Fan, and is believed to hold considerable potential for offshore oil and natural gas exploration. Its strategic significance, however, extends beyond hydrocarbon reserves to include electricity connectivity and the possibilities of developing renewable energy resources. India and Myanmar have made some progress in exploring and extracting energy resources from the Bay, although the pace and scale of development have varied considerably.
An embankment breach and flooding in Lokkhikhola village in Dacope upazila, Khulna, ahead of Cyclone Dana. Recurring storms, tidal pressures and coastal vulnerability underscore how shared environmental threats transcend national boundaries, even as regional cooperation continues to lag. Photo: Star

India's offshore exploration has gained momentum in recent years. In 2024, the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) achieved first oil production from its flagship deepwater project in the Krishna-Godavari Basin. Myanmar, meanwhile, moved relatively early in developing its offshore gas resources, with several major gas fields discovered in the Bay of Bengal region between 2004 and 2016. With Chinese support, commercial production from the Shwe gas project commenced, supplying markets including China, while Thailand also emerged as an important stakeholder in Myanmar's offshore gas sector. However, Myanmar's prolonged domestic political instability has constrained the country's ability to pursue further exploration and fully realise its offshore energy potential.

Bangladesh, despite its considerable offshore prospects, has been comparatively slower in developing its energy resources. In March 2024, the Government of Bangladesh and the Bangladesh Oil, Gas and Mineral Corporation (Petrobangla) announced an offshore bidding round for oil and gas exploration, the first such initiative since 2014. The government has also been considering a broader national offshore energy strategy to attract investment and encourage exploration. While the commercial viability of these initiatives will depend on several factors, including access to technology, investment, exploration capacity and the success of drilling operations, Dhaka increasingly views the Bay's energy potential as an important avenue for strengthening domestic energy security and supporting economic growth.

Bangladesh's offshore ambitions have, however, historically been complicated by maritime disputes. In 2009, an attempt by Bangladesh to explore gas resources near St Martin's Island, close to waters claimed by Myanmar, reportedly encountered resistance from the Myanmar Navy. The broader uncertainty surrounding maritime jurisdiction was subsequently addressed through the 2012 International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) ruling, which clarified Bangladesh's maritime entitlements and its rights within the exclusive economic zone (EEZ). Nevertheless, differences over maritime boundaries have not entirely disappeared. Bangladesh has also raised concerns at the United Nations regarding India's use of Base Point 89, which Dhaka argues lies approximately 2.3 nautical miles within Bangladeshi-claimed waters.

Despite optimistic estimates of the Bay's hydrocarbon potential, commercial extraction remains technologically demanding and economically uncertain. Deepwater exploration requires substantial investment, specialised technology and considerable risk-taking, factors that may constrain the pace of development, particularly for countries with limited financial and technological capacities. Nevertheless, the prospect of accessing offshore energy resources has heightened strategic competition among littoral states, each of which remains determined to protect its maritime entitlements and maximise its share of the Bay's economic potential.
BIMSTEC marks the 12th anniversary of the establishment of its Secretariat at a reception in Dhaka on 14 September 2026. Bangladesh currently chairs the seven-member regional grouping, which connects South and Southeast Asia through cooperation in areas including trade, connectivity, maritime transport, disaster management and the blue economy.

Alongside competition over marine resources and energy exploration, littoral states have increasingly prioritised naval modernisation and the expansion of port infrastructure. The growing dependence of these economies on maritime trade, combined with the Bay's strategic location along major international shipping routes, has reinforced the importance of maritime capabilities and connectivity. However, port development and naval expansion have not necessarily translated into greater regional cooperation. Instead, competing infrastructure projects, strategic calculations and commercial ambitions have intensified interstate rivalries. These developments have also attracted the growing involvement of extra-regional powers, whose economic, security and geopolitical interests have added further complexity to the maritime environment.

The Bay of Bengal is held together by shared ecological systems, energy resources, trade routes and historical connections, yet it is increasingly shaped by competing national interests and strategic calculations. Rather than facilitating a cohesive regional order, resource competition, uneven institutional cooperation, infrastructure rivalry and the growing presence of external powers have contributed to the political fragmentation of the region. The challenge, therefore, lies not merely in managing individual disputes but in developing cooperative mechanisms that can reconcile national interests with the shared responsibilities of governing an increasingly contested maritime space.

Given the shifts in the global balance of power, major players are turning their attention to the Bay's potential. With the involvement of major powers, the Bay of Bengal is witnessing a resurgence of geopolitical rivalries. China's rise as a global power has led to increased economic interests and the projection of its influence in the region. Notwithstanding these developments, there remains a possibility that the Bay of Bengal will once again emerge as a network facilitating the interstate movement of goods, people and ideas, albeit within a tighter legal framework.

Land and maritime transport corridors remain fraught

Ironically, political intransigence between India and Bangladesh has led to excellent cross-border facilities remaining closed, although there is hope that they will reopen sooner rather than later. Domestic instability within Myanmar has certainly prevented South Asia from establishing seamless road connectivity, leaving several projects stalled. India's Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project, intended to connect India's northeastern state of Mizoram with Myanmar and facilitate trade and commerce between the region and mainland India, has faced setbacks, as has the Trilateral Highway, which was intended to connect India to Thailand and which Dhaka had also planned to join.

Apart from its existing port facilities, Bangladesh is developing Matarbari, a deep seaport in the BoB. This has the potential to emerge as a crucial commercial hub in the BoB region, enabling the integration of industrial value chains with Northeast India. Located south of Chattogram Port, Matarbari Port holds commercial significance not just for Bangladesh and Japan, but also for India. Once operational, Matarbari Port will also support feeder vessel services from India's Kolkata and Haldia ports. This transshipment framework could facilitate efficient trade not only for India but also for landlocked neighbours such as Nepal and Bhutan. However, much of this potential remains unrealised and may continue to do so amid the region's current domestic challenges, particularly those affecting Bangladesh, Nepal and Myanmar. Sri Lanka has slowly been showing signs of stability and economic progress, but political instability has characterised this region and continues to hinder many planned projects and economic growth.

Arguably, political stability and better connectivity are imperative for developing trade and building export-oriented growth in many priority sectors, including agriculture, textiles and clothing, and fisheries, which are integral parts of the Bay region.

Limited institutional framework

The changing geopolitics has not been accompanied by regional development that adequately captures the essence of the region. Ironically, the region has seen a plethora of initiatives, such as BIMSTEC, IORA and India's MAHASAGAR, with different stages of activities and interests, yet none of these subregional groupings or national projects can fully represent the larger Bay of Bengal identity and its common interests. Conceived as a regional organisation to boost economic cooperation and free trade among countries in South Asia and Southeast Asia, BIMSTEC has been at the forefront of several cooperative efforts in the region.

BIMSTEC has been a slow starter, having finalised its Charter only after more than two decades, and its membership remains incomplete, as it does not include all the Bay of Bengal nations. Moreover, the priorities of members such as Bhutan and Nepal do not necessarily align fully with those of the maritime nations. It was a top-down exercise, and some members remain in the grouping largely because they do not wish to be excluded from a regional organisation, despite finding limited intrinsic convergence with other members. The seven core sectors of trade and investment; agriculture and food security; connectivity; science, technology and innovation; people-to-people contacts; security; and environment and climate change have seen progress, but nothing transformational. Two institutions, India's Information Fusion Centre and the BIMSTEC Centre for Weather and Climate, both based in India, have been well received by members. Sri Lanka is also developing another fusion centre, and it will be interesting to see how these institutions cooperate and work together. Given the growing volume of maritime traffic, additional fusion centres would be beneficial, but the final outcome would depend on how effectively these centres coordinate among themselves. BIMSTEC is still attempting to translate its geographical and economic potential into an effective regional institution. The Bay's future will depend not merely on who controls ports, shipping routes or maritime infrastructure, but also on whether its littoral states can develop mechanisms to manage common challenges.
An aerial view of the Matarbari deep-sea port project in Cox's Bazar. Backed by Japan as part of the Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt (BIG-B) initiative, port and connectivity projects hold considerable trade potential for Bangladesh, India and landlocked neighbours, even as domestic challenges and regional rivalries complicate their implementation. Photo: BSS

Given the Bay's proximity to the larger Indo-Pacific, regional and external powers are developing cooperative networks alongside competing strategies. The nation-states surrounding the Bay are keen to establish a rules-based maritime order, and BIMSTEC members are moving towards building a common maritime security architecture. The extra-regional nature of security threats has complicated cooperative efforts to develop a security framework in this region. Thus, developing a common security framework has become a major focus in recent years.

The IORA–BIMSTEC MoU of April 2025 has provided a starting point for collaboration on maritime security and economic connectivity, although transboundary ecological cooperation remains limited.

India has been a primary advocate of a rules-based maritime order, developing the concept of MAHASAGAR, which, among other priorities, emphasises the upgrading of ports such as Kolkata, Paradip and Visakhapatnam on the eastern seaboard. India has planned rapid economic development of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which will have a significant impact on the prosperity of the Bay of Bengal region. India has a dominant presence in the region and has also been able to position itself as a first responder in humanitarian disasters, with littoral nations frequently seeking its assistance in times of crisis.

Yet, despite the progress made through bilateral agreements and subregional groupings, one fundamental concern remains inadequately addressed: the region's growing ecological vulnerability and climate-related emergencies.
A Santos drilling rig explores natural gas reserves in Block 16 of the Bay of Bengal in 2011, highlighting the region's offshore energy potential and the growing strategic importance of its marine resources. Photo: Anurup Kanti Das

Environmental threats, by their very nature, transcend national boundaries, yet responses continue to be shaped largely by national priorities and capabilities. While Bay of Bengal countries have demonstrated a willingness to cooperate in the aftermath of natural disasters, such cooperation has largely remained reactive rather than institutionalised. The central question, therefore, is whether the countries bordering the Bay can develop a meaningful sense of regional identity and collective responsibility in confronting recurring cyclones, coastal vulnerability and rising sea levels, particularly in the absence of a robust regional institutional framework.

The Bay of Bengal region has faced the consequences of climate change, but its nations have not been able to coordinate their efforts and priorities. Governments continue to prioritise economic growth, energy security, industrial competitiveness and domestic political stability.

Climate governance

In recent months, several regional capitals have hosted substantive discussions on the Bay of Bengal, bringing together political, strategic, security, commercial and economic perspectives. These dialogues have engaged with a range of interconnected concerns and highlighted the growing strategic significance of the Bay. It is reasonable to argue that the region is not short of bilateral agreements, military exercises, diplomatic dialogues or regional institutions. What remains conspicuously absent, however, is an integrated mechanism capable of addressing the shared management of maritime spaces and resources and, more importantly, the mounting consequences of climate change. The Bay's rich biodiversity and ecologically sensitive coastal ecosystems, particularly the Sundarbans, which India and Bangladesh share, illustrate this institutional deficit. Even during periods of strong bilateral engagement, the two neighbours have failed to develop sufficiently coordinated approaches to conservation and ecological preservation. While geopolitical considerations, domestic political priorities and competing national interests often shape the choices of individual states, shared environmental challenges have not received the sustained collective attention they warrant.

At a time when countries are grappling with energy shortages, economic uncertainties and the wider consequences of international developments, a focused regional dialogue on ecological security may appear somewhat removed from immediate political and economic priorities. Yet, this is precisely why it demands urgent attention. Climate change is not a challenge that individual countries can effectively confront in isolation, nor can its consequences be contained within national boundaries. The Bay of Bengal countries must therefore recognise the need to pool their knowledge, institutional capacities, technological capabilities and financial resources to address this shared vulnerability.
Fishing boats at sunset on the Bay of Bengal. Long a vital corridor linking South and Southeast Asia through trade, migration and shared livelihoods, the Bay is increasingly shaped by competing strategic interests and pressing ecological challenges. File photo: Mohiuddin Ahmed Sagor

Undoubtedly, there is growing international recognition of climate change issues and increasing awareness among governments and civil society, but the inability to deliver on commitments has always been a problem in this sector. While all recognise the crisis, meaningful change cannot be achieved through individual efforts alone.

Ultimately, the region's ability to build a meaningful cooperative framework may depend as much on its collective response to ecological threats as on its engagement with the more conventional concerns of trade, connectivity and maritime security. Can ecological security provide the Bay of Bengal with a compelling foundation for building a shared regional identity? The Bay of Bengal region needs to establish its own climate dialogues that would consolidate its positions and strengthen its negotiating capacity vis-à-vis the developed world.

Dr Sreeradha Datta is a professor at the Jindal School of International Affairs, O.P. Jindal Global University, and a non-resident senior fellow at ISAS-NUS, Singapore.

The growing dependence of these economies on maritime trade, combined with the Bay's strategic location along major international shipping routes, has reinforced the importance of maritime capabilities and connectivity. However, port development and naval expansion have not necessarily translated into greater regional cooperation. Instead, competing infrastructure projects, strategic calculations and commercial ambitions have intensified interstate rivalries. These developments have also attracted the growing involvement of extra-regional powers, whose economic, security and geopolitical interests have added further complexity to the maritime environment.

The Bay of Bengal is held together by shared ecological systems, energy resources, trade routes and historical connections, yet it is increasingly shaped by competing national interests and strategic calculations. Rather than facilitating a cohesive regional order, resource competition, uneven institutional cooperation, infrastructure rivalry and the growing presence of external powers have contributed to the political fragmentation of the region. The challenge, therefore, lies not merely in managing individual disputes but in developing cooperative mechanisms that can reconcile national interests with the shared responsibilities of governing an increasingly contested maritime space.

Given the shifts in the global balance of power, major players are turning their attention to the Bay's potential. With the involvement of major powers, the Bay of Bengal is witnessing a resurgence of geopolitical rivalries. China's rise as a global power has led to increased economic interests and the projection of its influence in the region. Notwithstanding these developments, there remains a possibility that the Bay of Bengal will once again emerge as a network facilitating the interstate movement of goods, people and ideas, albeit within a tighter legal framework.

Land and maritime transport corridors remain fraught

Ironically, political intransigence between India and Bangladesh has led to excellent cross-border facilities remaining closed, although there is hope that they will reopen sooner rather than later. Domestic instability within Myanmar has certainly prevented South Asia from establishing seamless road connectivity, leaving several projects stalled. India's Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project, intended to connect India's northeastern state of Mizoram with Myanmar and facilitate trade and commerce between the region and mainland India, has faced setbacks, as has the Trilateral Highway, which was intended to connect India to Thailand and which Dhaka had also planned to join.
A distributary of the Rupsha River winds through mangrove cover near the Sundarbans in Dacope, Khulna, on 30 March 2026. Shared coastal ecosystems such as the Sundarbans highlight the need for coordinated transboundary conservation and collective climate action. Photo: AFP

Apart from its existing port facilities, Bangladesh is developing Matarbari, a deep seaport in the BoB. This has the potential to emerge as a crucial commercial hub in the BoB region, enabling the integration of industrial value chains with Northeast India. Located south of Chattogram Port, Matarbari Port holds commercial significance not just for Bangladesh and Japan, but also for India. Once operational, Matarbari Port will also support feeder vessel services from India's Kolkata and Haldia ports. This transshipment framework could facilitate efficient trade not only for India but also for landlocked neighbours such as Nepal and Bhutan. However, much of this potential remains unrealised and may continue to do so amid the region's current domestic challenges, particularly those affecting Bangladesh, Nepal and Myanmar. Sri Lanka has slowly been showing signs of stability and economic progress, but political instability has characterised this region and continues to hinder many planned projects and economic growth.

Arguably, political stability and better connectivity are imperative for developing trade and building export-oriented growth in many priority sectors, including agriculture, textiles and clothing, and fisheries, which are integral parts of the Bay region.

Limited institutional framework

The changing geopolitics has not been accompanied by regional development that adequately captures the essence of the region. Ironically, the region has seen a plethora of initiatives, such as BIMSTEC, IORA and India's MAHASAGAR, with different stages of activities and interests, yet none of these subregional groupings or national projects can fully represent the larger Bay of Bengal identity and its common interests. Conceived as a regional organisation to boost economic cooperation and free trade among countries in South Asia and Southeast Asia, BIMSTEC has been at the forefront of several cooperative efforts in the region.

BIMSTEC has been a slow starter, having finalised its Charter only after more than two decades, and its membership remains incomplete, as it does not include all the Bay of Bengal nations. Moreover, the priorities of members such as Bhutan and Nepal do not necessarily align fully with those of the maritime nations. It was a top-down exercise, and some members remain in the grouping largely because they do not wish to be excluded from a regional organisation, despite finding limited intrinsic convergence with other members. The seven core sectors of trade and investment; agriculture and food security; connectivity; science, technology and innovation; people-to-people contacts; security; and environment and climate change have seen progress, but nothing transformational. Two institutions, India's Information Fusion Centre and the BIMSTEC Centre for Weather and Climate, both based in India, have been well received by members. Sri Lanka is also developing another fusion centre, and it will be interesting to see how these institutions cooperate and work together. Given the growing volume of maritime traffic, additional fusion centres would be beneficial, but the final outcome would depend on how effectively these centres coordinate among themselves. BIMSTEC is still attempting to translate its geographical and economic potential into an effective regional institution. The Bay's future will depend not merely on who controls ports, shipping routes or maritime infrastructure, but also on whether its littoral states can develop mechanisms to manage common challenges.
An aerial view of the Matarbari deep-sea port project in Cox's Bazar. Backed by Japan as part of the Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt (BIG-B) initiative, port and connectivity projects hold considerable trade potential for Bangladesh, India and landlocked neighbours, even as domestic challenges and regional rivalries complicate their implementation. Photo: BSS

Given the Bay's proximity to the larger Indo-Pacific, regional and external powers are developing cooperative networks alongside competing strategies. The nation-states surrounding the Bay are keen to establish a rules-based maritime order, and BIMSTEC members are moving towards building a common maritime security architecture. The extra-regional nature of security threats has complicated cooperative efforts to develop a security framework in this region. Thus, developing a common security framework has become a major focus in recent years.

The IORA–BIMSTEC MoU of April 2025 has provided a starting point for collaboration on maritime security and economic connectivity, although transboundary ecological cooperation remains limited.

India has been a primary advocate of a rules-based maritime order, developing the concept of MAHASAGAR, which, among other priorities, emphasises the upgrading of ports such as Kolkata, Paradip and Visakhapatnam on the eastern seaboard. India has planned rapid economic development of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which will have a significant impact on the prosperity of the Bay of Bengal region. India has a dominant presence in the region and has also been able to position itself as a first responder in humanitarian disasters, with littoral nations frequently seeking its assistance in times of crisis.

Yet, despite the progress made through bilateral agreements and subregional groupings, one fundamental concern remains inadequately addressed: the region's growing ecological vulnerability and climate-related emergencies.
A Santos drilling rig explores natural gas reserves in Block 16 of the Bay of Bengal in 2011, highlighting the region's offshore energy potential and the growing strategic importance of its marine resources. Photo: Anurup Kanti Das

Environmental threats, by their very nature, transcend national boundaries, yet responses continue to be shaped largely by national priorities and capabilities. While Bay of Bengal countries have demonstrated a willingness to cooperate in the aftermath of natural disasters, such cooperation has largely remained reactive rather than institutionalised. The central question, therefore, is whether the countries bordering the Bay can develop a meaningful sense of regional identity and collective responsibility in confronting recurring cyclones, coastal vulnerability and rising sea levels, particularly in the absence of a robust regional institutional framework.

The Bay of Bengal region has faced the consequences of climate change, but its nations have not been able to coordinate their efforts and priorities. Governments continue to prioritise economic growth, energy security, industrial competitiveness and domestic political stability.

Climate governance

In recent months, several regional capitals have hosted substantive discussions on the Bay of Bengal, bringing together political, strategic, security, commercial and economic perspectives. These dialogues have engaged with a range of interconnected concerns and highlighted the growing strategic significance of the Bay. It is reasonable to argue that the region is not short of bilateral agreements, military exercises, diplomatic dialogues or regional institutions. What remains conspicuously absent, however, is an integrated mechanism capable of addressing the shared management of maritime spaces and resources and, more importantly, the mounting consequences of climate change. The Bay's rich biodiversity and ecologically sensitive coastal ecosystems, particularly the Sundarbans, which India and Bangladesh share, illustrate this institutional deficit. Even during periods of strong bilateral engagement, the two neighbours have failed to develop sufficiently coordinated approaches to conservation and ecological preservation. While geopolitical considerations, domestic political priorities and competing national interests often shape the choices of individual states, shared environmental challenges have not received the sustained collective attention they warrant.

At a time when countries are grappling with energy shortages, economic uncertainties and the wider consequences of international developments, a focused regional dialogue on ecological security may appear somewhat removed from immediate political and economic priorities. Yet, this is precisely why it demands urgent attention. Climate change is not a challenge that individual countries can effectively confront in isolation, nor can its consequences be contained within national boundaries. The Bay of Bengal countries must therefore recognise the need to pool their knowledge, institutional capacities, technological capabilities and financial resources to address this shared vulnerability.

Undoubtedly, there is growing international recognition of climate change issues and increasing awareness among governments and civil society, but the inability to deliver on commitments has always been a problem in this sector. While all recognise the crisis, meaningful change cannot be achieved through individual efforts alone.

Ultimately, the region's ability to build a meaningful cooperative framework may depend as much on its collective response to ecological threats as on its engagement with the more conventional concerns of trade, connectivity and maritime security. Can ecological security provide the Bay of Bengal with a compelling foundation for building a shared regional identity? The Bay of Bengal region needs to establish its own climate dialogues that would consolidate its positions and strengthen its negotiating capacity vis-à-vis the developed world.

item.title: The Daily Star – The quiet science of loving and being loved by pets
item.description:
For many people, pets offer more than companionship. They provide comfort during difficult times, ease loneliness and give their owners a sense of purpose through the everyday responsibility of caring for another living being.

But how much of that comfort translates into measurable mental and physical health benefits? Research suggests pets can improve mood and encourage physical activity, although evidence of lasting mental health benefits remains mixed. These relationships can also bring anxiety, financial strain and grief.

For Naziba Bashar, a journalist and animal rescuer from Dhanmondi, Dhaka, that emotional connection is captured in the story of a frightened kitten she spent nearly three hours trying to rescue.

Barely three weeks old, malnourished and anaemic, the kitten had hidden beneath a car in a garage. Naziba crawled after her, enduring scratches and bites before finally catching her. She carried the kitten upstairs, offered her food and gently stroked her head.
Doi grooms a tiny kitten rescued from a nearby garage, helping the newcomer feel more comfortable.

Soon, the kitten nestled into Naziba's hair and fell asleep.

"There's a particular breath animals sometimes take when they finally surrender to sleep. A long, soft exhale," Naziba recalled. To her, it sounded almost as though the kitten was saying, "Okay, maa is here now. I can rest."

She named her Obi. A year later, Obi is still with her.

Across Bangladesh, pet owners describe similar bonds: animals waiting at doors, seeking familiar laps or offering quiet company during illness and emotional distress.

But while these experiences suggest companionship can make difficult moments more bearable, scientists caution that keeping a pet is not, in itself, a treatment for mental or physical illness.

A language without words

Dr Mekhala Sarkar, a psychiatrist at the National Institute of Mental Health in Dhaka, said emotional connections need not depend on speech.
A kitten rests on its caregiver's lap, enjoying a gentle stroke. Such everyday moments can help build trust between animals and their owners.

"We think communication happens only through words. But body language, expressions and the eyes are also important ways of communicating," she added.

Caring for animals, according to Mekhala, can provide opportunities to express affection and a sense of responsibility, reinforcing a person's sense of self-worth. However, such benefits cannot be assumed for everyone.

A study published in the Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery in August 2026 examined hormonal responses in 20 pet cats in China. Calm interactions were associated with higher oxytocin and lower cortisol levels, while forced contact showed the opposite pattern.

Although the study examined cats rather than their owners, it highlighted the importance of respecting an animal's comfort and individual preferences.

Dr Nusrat Jahan, chief veterinary consultant at Bangladesh Animal Care Centre in Dhaka, said animals have different preferences for physical affection. Hissing, growling, scratching or turning away can signal discomfort, which owners should recognise and respect.
Obi (left), Ghurni (back), Mini (front) and Chini (right) settle together on a bed, sharing a quiet moment of comfort and companionship.

Someone to come home to

Photojournalist Orchid Chakma, who lives alone in Dhaka, had never intended to keep a cat.

That changed on 30 June, when he rescued a sick kitten crying near the road below his balcony.

He named her Mao. Initially overwhelmed by her care, including treatment for vomiting and diarrhoea, Orchid considered putting her up for adoption. Instead, he gradually grew attached.

His father had died less than a year before the interview, and the apartment felt empty after his parents were no longer living with him. He had also begun spending most of his time between work and home.

Mao did not erase his grief, but caring for her gave him companionship and a daily routine. He says he now feels less irritable and enjoys spending time playing with her.

Mahima Jenin Shara, a corporate professional living in Gulshan, Dhaka, shares a similar attachment to her six cats.

Her youngest, seven-month-old Mishu, begins meowing when Mahima reaches the corridor outside her flat. Another cat, Pappu, sometimes settles on her chest and purrs when she is upset.

Caring for them, Mahima said, has changed her evenings and made her more eager to return home.

A study published in Frontiers in Psychology in June 2026 followed 188 dog and cat owners in the Netherlands and Belgium, recording their mood, stress levels and interactions up to 10 times daily over five days.

Pet interactions were associated with more positive and fewer negative feelings, but researchers found no general evidence that they reduced the emotional impact of stress. The observational study could not establish causation.
A cat sits in front of a television during a football match, capturing a quiet moment of everyday life in a pet-friendly home.

What the research shows

A November 2025 study by Mohammad Bayazid Bostami, an assistant professor at Chattogram Veterinary and Animal Sciences University, and colleagues surveyed 328 pet owners in Dhaka.

Some 48.78 per cent reported feeling less angry, lonely, restless or depressed in connection with pet ownership, while 41.46 per cent reported no noticeable change in the health outcomes examined.

Another 20.73 per cent reported health complaints, including allergies, asthma or ringworm.

The findings, however, relied on owners' accounts, without clinical assessments or a comparison group of non-owners.

Broader research presents a similarly mixed picture.

An April 2025 review of 116 studies by Katherine Northrope and colleagues at La Trobe University in Australia found that stronger attachment to pets was associated with better mental health in some studies, poorer outcomes in others and no clear relationship in many.

A January 2026 study published in PLOS One, involving 975 adults in the United Kingdom, found that among participants who had lost both a beloved pet and a person, 21 per cent identified the pet's death as their most distressing bereavement. Some also reported symptoms of prolonged grief.
Mini, the black-and-white cat, stretches out in a peaceful sleep, while Ghurni rests beside Olive, the little orange kitten, as the three share a cosy afternoon together.

Mekhala said losing an animal can be a genuine form of bereavement. Persistent distress that disrupts daily life may require professional support.

"Pets can never replace people," she said, emphasising the importance of maintaining meaningful connections with family and friends.

The physical benefits may be more measurable, particularly among dog owners.

An August 2026 study in Scientific Reports, involving 258 adults in China, found that 132 dog owners averaged 1,579 more daily steps and 12.2 more minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity than 126 non-owners at baseline.

Dog owners also reported more favourable mental health scores during follow-up, although researchers could not rule out the possibility that more active people were already inclined to own dogs.
Patlu, an affectionate cat who loved staying close to her caregiver.

What affection asks in return

For Nawshin Mahpara Tripti and her husband, Mehedi Hasan Shitol, caring for a sick kitten meant sacrificing their plans to furnish their new home.

Shortly after adopting Danish, the couple discovered that he was seriously ill and struggled to walk.

For weeks, they took him for veterinary treatment, sometimes twice daily, before continuing his care at home.

Their savings went towards his treatment instead of furniture.

"I don't have furniture at home, but at least my cat can walk around now," Nawshin said.

The experience also changed how she handles disagreements, as she worries that shouting might frighten Danish.

Mahima understands that anxiety. When two of her cats, Pappu and Rani, became seriously ill, she arranged intensive treatment for them. Both survived, but she continues to worry about who would care for her animals if anything happened to her or her parents.

For Abdur Razzak, a 54-year-old businessman from Patuakhali, keeping birds for nearly two decades has brought companionship alongside considerable responsibility.
Dressed in a striped sweater, Shontu explores a small rooftop garden beside a potted plant.

At one point, he cared for 80 to 90 pairs of birds, including parrots, mynas, lovebirds and pigeons. Feeding and looking after them often restricted his ability to travel, prompting him to reduce their number as he grew older. Such responsibilities extend beyond providing food and shelter.

Nusrat said vaccination, parasite prevention, hygiene and veterinary care are essential to protecting both animals and their owners.

Affection, she stressed, must be accompanied by appropriate care.

The grief that stays

For animal rescuer KN Deya of Shyamoli, Dhaka, caring for cats has shaped family decisions, finances and everyday routines.

She and her family currently care for seven cats, all rescued animals or their offspring.

During a prolonged illness in 2025, Deya spent around three months in and out of hospital and was subsequently bedridden for weeks. Her cat Shundori, usually demanding, became unusually quiet and often stayed beside her.

But Deya's strongest memories are of Patlu, a calico cat she lost in 2022.
Shontu, an orange-and-white cat, perches on a tree branch, looking curiously at his surroundings.

During seven months of working in Jashore in 2020, Deya regularly spoke to her family in Dhaka over video calls. Patlu would meow at the sound of her voice.

Two years later, Patlu developed a serious lung illness. Three other family cats recovered, but Patlu's condition deteriorated despite treatment.

Patlu died in Deya's arms.

"For about a week, I'd start to affectionately call for her and then stop abruptly, remembering she was gone," Deya recalled.

Naziba knows that grief.

She lost Leo after nearly 20 years together. Another rescue ended with the deaths of an injured office cat, Puri, and all five of her kittens, despite efforts by Naziba and her colleagues to save them.

"Love isn't always enough to keep someone alive. That's an incredibly difficult truth to accept," she said.

The losses left her questioning whether she could have done more, while other rescued animals continued to depend on her.

She also remembers people dismissing her grief with remarks such as "It was just a cat" or "You have so many others."

For Naziba, affection and responsibility have become inseparable.

"I may have given my animals a home," she said, "but in more ways than I can count, they've given me belonging, purpose and emotional safety."

Tamanna Yesmin Maria is a reporter at The Daily Star. She can be reached at [email protected].

item.title: The Daily Star – From Airbus to energy: The expanding Bangladesh–France partnership
item.description:
Jean-Marc Séré-Charlet, French Ambassador to Bangladesh, speaks to The Daily Star about the evolving Bangladesh–France partnership, opportunities to expand bilateral trade and investment, Bangladesh’s economic diversification and LDC graduation, cooperation in renewable energy, higher education and the Indo-Pacific, longstanding cultural ties, and France’s perspective on Bangladesh’s democratic transition and institutional reforms.

The Daily Star (TDS): France has recently seen student-led protests over government policies and political accountability. How do you assess the grievances behind these demonstrations and the government's response?

Jean-Marc Séré-Charlet (JMSC): France has a long tradition of demonstrations. The French Revolution itself began with demonstrations, and the right to demonstrate is protected by our Constitution. People must be free to exercise this right and call for change.

What matters is that legitimate demonstrations remain free from violence. We have seen small groups join protests to loot or cause disturbances rather than express legitimate demands. Following the serious outbreak of violence on 17 October, the government had to address the law-and-order situation while allowing people to continue demonstrating.

TDS: This year marks the 50th death anniversary of André Malraux, who supported Bangladesh's Liberation War in 1971. How can France and Bangladesh build on their historical and cultural ties to strengthen cooperation in culture, education and people-to-people exchanges?

JMSC: Culture is central to our cooperation. France values its heritage, arts and creativity, and began protecting its heritage through legislation as early as 1830s. André Malraux, our first minister of culture, reflected that commitment. We want to share it with our partners.

Our cultural relationship with Bangladesh goes back a long way. The Alliance Française in Dhaka was established in 1959, and the one in Chittagong in 1965. These are places where our cultures meet, and the exchanges predate Bangladesh's independence.

We have government-to-government agreements on cultural cooperation and archaeology. Recently, curators from Bangladesh spent two months at the Musée du Quai Branly in Paris. They shared experiences with their French counterparts. We want more such exchanges.

I would also include higher education in this wider understanding of culture. We want students and researchers from both countries to meet and work together. We already have Bangladeshi students in France, but we hope to welcome more. Student exchanges are a long-term investment because they help our societies understand each other better.
Jean-Marc Séré-Charlet, French Ambassador to Bangladesh

TDS: France is an important European market for Bangladesh's ready-made garments, while Biman's decision to purchase Airbus aircraft marks a new chapter in bilateral economic relations. What opportunities do you see for expanding trade, attracting French investment and diversifying Bangladesh's exports?

JMSC: First, the Airbus agreement is a success, but it is important to recognise that it is Biman's own strategic decision. The discussions began years ago at Biman's request. The airline wanted a mixed fleet to strengthen its autonomy rather than depend on one supplier. Many international airlines operate both Airbus and Boeing aircraft.

The choice of the A350-900 is significant because of its range. It would give Biman the capacity to operate directly from Dhaka to the east coast of the United States without a stop. Aircraft purchases create partnerships that last much longer than a year or two.

We see great potential in Bangladesh. French companies are impressed by the quality and responsiveness of its ready-made garment industry.
